title: Letter to John Locke, 30 June 1691, on the 'phantasm' of the sun (in Lord King, The Life of John Locke)
author: Isaac Newton
edition_cited: Lord King, The Life of John Locke, with Extracts from his Correspondence, Journals and Common-place Books, new ed., London: Colburn and Bentley, 1830, vol. 1, pp. 404-408; archive.org lifeofjohnlockew01king
seen_via: Printed in Lord King's Life of John Locke (1830), vol. 1; the saved file is that whole volume
locator_hints: Vol. 1, printed pp. 404-408: letter headed 'Cambridge, June 30th, 1691'; the account begins 'The observation you mention in Mr. Boyle's book of Colours, I once made upon myself with the hazard of my eyes'
In the saved file at roughly lines 14095-14185
summary: Newton tells Locke what happened when he looked briefly at the sun in a mirror with one eye and then watched the after-image in a dark corner, three times. As the 'phantasm of light and colours' was almost gone he 'intended his fancy' on it and found it returning as vivid as at first; when he stopped, it vanished. Thereafter he could bring it back in the dark by attending 'as when a man looks earnestly to see any thing which is difficult to be seen', more easily each time, until a bright round spot appeared on any bright object, and in the unexposed eye too. He shut himself in a darkened room for three days to recover; for months the image returned whenever he thought of it, even in bed at midnight.
why_relevant: A first-person report of a physically induced afterimage becoming light that is summoned by attention alone, transferring to the unexposed eye and persisting for months, with a plain account of the damage and of what reversed it. It bears on every afterimage-plus-attention method in this stream.

notes: Safety: sun_gazing; Newton says he did it 'with the hazard of my eyes' and could not read or write for days. It is a warning as much as a method. Outside the stream's nominal 20th-21st century range, but included as the classic non-lineage report on this mechanism.
